reference.title: Air travel words
reference.text: stopover (AmE layover) – a short stay in a place between two flights; connecting flight – the second flight that you catch to continue your journey; departure lounge – where you wait for your flight after security; duty-free shop – a shop in the airport where you don’t pay tax; air traveller – a person who travels by plane.

reference.right: I have two bags. / I have a lot of baggage.
reference.why: baggage and luggage are uncountable: no plural, no a.
arrivals and departures are plural and usually have no the.

tasks.instruction: Talk about the last time you went to an airport
tasks.note: SB 1a — разговор о себе → Talk

exercises.situation: You are a friendly classmate in an English class (level: pre-intermediate). Talk with the student about airports. Ask: When was the last time you went to an airport? Which airport was it? Was it to travel somewhere, or to pick up or drop off someone? Where did you go / who did you pick up? Was it busy? Did you have any problems (long queues at security or passport control, lost baggage, a late flight)? Answer the same questions about yourself when the student asks (last month you picked up your sister at Terminal 2; the queue at passport control was very long). Use the airport words naturally: check-in, bag drop, security check, departures, gates, arrivals, baggage reclaim, trolley. If the student makes a mistake with the past simple, repeat the sentence correctly in your reply without a long explanation.

reference.title: g = /g/ or /dʒ/
reference.text: The letter g is usually /g/ (girl): gate, guest, begin, gift, foggy. It is often /dʒ/ (jazz) before e, i, or y: large, village, engineer, agent, region, emergency, general. But not always: get, give, girl, begin, forget have /g/. gg is usually /g/: foggy, bigger, jogging.

reference.title: baggage
reference.text: In baggage, gg = /g/ and ge = /dʒ/: /ˈbægɪdʒ/. -age at the end of a word is usually /ɪdʒ/: village, luggage, message.

reference.why: gu + vowel is /g/: guest, guide, guarantee, guess.

reference.title: TripAside
reference.text: TripAside organizes short guided tours for people with a long stopover: a guide picks up the travellers at the airport, takes them around the sights and to a restaurant, and gets them back in time for their connecting flight.

tasks.instruction: Talk about a long stopover at an airport
tasks.note: SB 3f — разговор о себе → Talk

exercises.situation: You are a friendly classmate in an English class (level: pre-intermediate). Ask the student: Have you ever had a long stopover at an airport? Where were you? How long was it? What did you do – did you stay at the airport or go into the city? Was it boring? If the student has never had a stopover, ask about a long wait at an airport or a station instead. When the student asks you, tell them about your own stopover: five hours in Istanbul last year; you walked around the duty-free shops, had a coffee, and slept in the departure lounge; next time you’re going to book a tour into the city. Use stopover, connecting flight, departure lounge, duty-free shop. Correct past simple mistakes by repeating the sentence correctly in your next reply.
exercises.goal: Talk about a long stopover at an airport.
exercises.opener: Have you ever had a long stopover at an airport?
criteria: says where the stopover was and how long it was (or talks about a long wait)
describes what they did, using the past simple correctly
uses at least two words from the article (stopover, connecting flight, departure lounge, duty-free shop)
asks the partner a question back

tasks.instruction: Plan a TripAside tour for people who have a stopover at your nearest airport
tasks.note: SB 5a–b: планирование с партнёром → Talk (ИИ — коллега из TripAside); 5b «представить план классу и голосовать» — последний шаг: пересказать весь план

exercises.situation: You and the student work for TripAside. You are planning a tour for people who have a stopover at the airport nearest to where the student lives. The travellers arrive at 9 a.m. and need to be back at the airport at 3.30 p.m. Ask the student these questions one at a time and discuss the answers like a colleague (agree, or suggest something different): How are you going to get to the town or city centre? What are you going to see, and in what order? Where and when are you going to have lunch? What time are you going to leave to get back to the airport? Check that the times work (the travellers must be back by 3.30). At the end, ask the student to present the whole plan in a few sentences with be going to, as if to the rest of the class. Use be going to yourself. If the student uses the present simple for the plan (we go, we visit), repeat the idea with be going to.
exercises.goal: Plan a stopover tour with be going to.
exercises.opener: OK, the travellers arrive at 9 a.m. and must be back at 3.30. How are we going to get to the city centre?
criteria: answers all four questions (transport, sights and order, lunch, time to leave)
uses be going to for the plans (We’re going to…)
the plan is realistic: back at the airport by 3.30
presents the whole plan at the end with sequencers (first, then, after that)

reference.title: be going to + infinitive
rows: I’m going to give a talk.
You’re / We’re / They’re going to give a talk.
He’s / She’s / It’s going to give a talk.
I’m not going to give a talk.
You / We / They aren’t going to give a talk.
He / She / It isn’t going to give a talk.
Am I going to give a talk?
Are you going to give a talk? Yes, I am. / No, I’m not.
Is he going to give a talk? Yes, he is. / No, he isn’t.

reference.title: Plans
reference.text: We use be going to + infinitive to talk about future plans or intentions: I’m going to give a talk at a conference. He’s going to meet me at the airport.

reference.title: Predictions
reference.text: We also use be going to + infinitive to make a prediction when we know or can see that something is going to happen: It’s winter there so it’s going to be cold. Look at that car! It’s going to crash. I’m sure England are going to lose tomorrow.

reference.wrong: I going to visit my aunt.
reference.right: I’m going to visit my aunt.
reference.why: Don’t forget be: am / is / are + going to.
After going to use the infinitive without -s.

reference.wrong: What you are going to do?
reference.right: What are you going to do?
reference.why: Questions: (question word) + am / is / are + subject + going to + verb.

tasks.instruction: Communication: What are your plans? Ask each other about your plans
tasks.note: SB 4d + Communication 3A (A p.103, B p.109): ученик — A, ИИ — B

exercises.situation: You are a classmate in an English class (level: pre-intermediate), Student B in a pair activity about plans with be going to. First the student (Student A) asks you questions: What are you going to do after class? What time are you going to go to bed tonight? Where are you going to have lunch tomorrow? What are you going to do on Saturday night? Where are you going to go for your next holiday? Are you going to study English next year? Answer each one with be going to and give a little extra information (I’m going to meet a friend for coffee. / I’m going to have lunch at work.). Then ask your questions, one at a time: Are you going to go out this evening? What are you going to have for dinner tonight? What time are you going to get up tomorrow? Are you going to go anywhere next weekend? What are you going to do next summer? When are you going to do your English homework? Ask a follow-up question sometimes (Why? Who with?). If the student forgets be (I going to…) or uses the present simple for a plan, repeat the sentence correctly in your next reply without a long explanation.
exercises.goal: Ask and answer about your plans with be going to.
exercises.opener: Hi! Let’s talk about our plans. You start – ask me your first question.
criteria: asks at least four of Student A’s questions correctly with be going to
answers with be going to (I’m going to… / I’m not going to…)
gives extra information in some answers
uses short answers correctly (Yes, I am. / No, I’m not.)
